title: Solved by walking
hookLine: a Latin saying, later attached to Diogenes: it is solved by walking

cards: An hour on the same problem, and nothing. The email you can't word. The decision about the job, the move, the conversation.
You've made lists. You've asked three friends. Your head feels like a room with the windows shut.
Then you give up, go out to buy milk, and somewhere around the second corner the answer just arrives, as if it was waiting for your legs. People have noticed this long enough to give it a Latin name.
A new week starts today: walking, the body, and sleep.

teach.b: Solvitur ambulando means it is solved by walking. The story it's attached to is older than the phrase.

In ancient Greece, the philosopher Zeno of Elea built well-known puzzles meant to show that motion is impossible: to cross a room, you must first cross half of it, and half of that half, forever, so how do you ever arrive?
The story goes that when someone argued this to Diogenes the Cynic, he didn't answer. He stood up and walked around. Diogenes Laertius, a biographer writing long afterward, tells a version of it.
The Latin tag came much later again, and people have pinned it on Diogenes ever since, though Diogenes spoke Greek, so the words were never his. But the idea caught on, and grew.
Some philosophers took long walks to think. Nietzsche wrote that only thoughts that come from walking have any value. Modern science has poked at it too.

In a 2014 Stanford study, people came up with more creative ideas while walking than while sitting, even walking on a treadmill facing a blank wall. It was a lab task, not a life decision, so it's a clue, not a promise.
Still, notice what walking does. It moves the body, so the mind loosens its grip. It gives your eyes something new every few steps.
And it sets a gentle rhythm, left, right, that your thoughts can ride on. Sometimes you don't solve it.

how: Writers, philosophers and plenty of others take a walk to think a problem through, and the Latin phrase solvitur ambulando is sometimes quoted to describe it.

o: a problem gets solved by walking

games.q: you're Diogenes. someone argues, cleverly, that motion is impossible. what do you do?
games.why: in the story he says nothing and walks. the answer to an argument about motion is to move.

practice: Let one question come up, something real you've been chewing on, and say it once, clearly, inside. Then set it down, the way you'd put a bag on the floor, and feel your feet.
Picture a ten-minute walk later, the question riding along but not driving, and for now just breathe with it nearby.

wordCard.voice: Solvitur ambulando. Latin for it is solved by walking, a saying pinned on Diogenes, who answered an argument by getting up and moving. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin: it is solved (solvitur) by walking (ambulando). a later tag, not Diogenes' own words; he spoke Greek.

carryVoice: Your line: walk it out. Some answers come on foot. One hundred twenty-nine days, and counting.
